chapters.label: In code, and which to use

scenes.narration: The exam office has a thousand candidates in a sorted list, and a student asks: am I on it? Checking every name could take a thousand looks. There’s a way that needs only ten.
Today: searching, one by one or by halving.
Linear search checks each item in turn, from the start. It works on any list, sorted or not. If the item is found, return its position; if the loop ends without finding it, return minus one.

How much work is that? If the item is last, or missing, linear search looks at every item. For a thousand names, that’s a thousand comparisons. For a million, a million. The work grows in step with the list.

Binary search is cleverer, but it needs a sorted list. Look at the middle item. If it’s what you want, stop. If your target is bigger, throw away the lower half; if smaller, the upper half. Repeat on what’s left.

Each step halves what’s left. A thousand, five hundred, two hundred and fifty, and so on: about ten steps to reach one. A million needs only about twenty. That’s why dictionaries and contact lists are kept in order.
Quick check! Which list can binary search use: the names in the order pupils arrived, or the names in alphabetical order?
The alphabetical list. Binary search throws half away on every step, and that’s only safe if the list is sorted. On an unsorted list, it can miss a name that’s really there.
In code, keep two markers, lo and hi, around the part that’s left. Each time round, look at the middle. Move lo up or hi down. When lo passes hi, the target isn’t there.

So which should you use? For a short list, or one that isn’t sorted, linear search is simple and fine. For a big sorted list searched again and again, binary search wins by miles. Sorting first costs time, so it pays only when you search often.
In the app, open Guess the number and choose one to a thousand. Race one by one against halving, and watch halving finish in about ten steps. Then read the table: a million adds only ten more.
Your turn. A sorted list has a thousand and twenty-four names. At most, how many looks does binary search need?
About eleven. Remember: linear search checks every item, and works on any list. Binary search halves what’s left, but needs a sorted list. For a thousand items, a thousand looks against about ten.
Try it yourself: take a dictionary or a phone’s contact list, and find a word by halving: open the middle, then keep the half it must be in. Count your looks. Then try one by one!

checkpoints.prompt: Which list can binary search use?

options.text: Names in the order pupils arrived

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — halving only works if everything below the middle is smaller and everything above is bigger.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — binary search needs a sorted list; otherwise throwing half away might throw away the target.

checkpoints.prompt: A sorted list has 1,024 names. At most, how many looks does binary search need?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — halving 1,024 reaches 1 after 10 halvings, plus the final look: 11.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — each look halves what’s left: 1,024 down to 1 is 10 halvings, so 11 looks.
